key_insight: This paper generalizes social laws from deterministic multi-agent planning to stochastic, reward-based environments, giving a way to check whether coordination rules remain reliable when outcomes are uncertain. It introduces robustness notions such as α-robustness to quantify how well a social law protects agent performance under randomness.
problem_solved: Multi-agent systems often interfere with each other, causing unstable or degraded performance in environments where actions and outcomes are stochastic. The paper addresses how to define, evaluate, and verify coordination rules that prevent interference while remaining robust to uncertainty.
method: Formulates social laws for stochastic, reward-based multi-agent settings instead of only deterministic goal-based ones.
Defines robustness criteria, including α-robustness, to measure how reliably a social law preserves performance.
Provides a formal verification framework to assess whether a proposed social law holds under different stochastic conditions.
impact: This gives AI/ML practitioners a principled way to design coordination rules for multi-agent systems operating in noisy, real-world environments. It can improve reliability, reduce harmful interference, and make multi-agent behavior easier to reason about and deploy.
visual_elements: A side-by-side diagram comparing deterministic social laws vs. stochastic social laws.
A flowchart showing agents, environment randomness, coordination rule, and robustness check.
A robustness curve or bar chart illustrating α-robustness across different noise levels.
An icon-based illustration of multiple agents avoiding collisions or interference in a shared environment.
paper_title: Social Laws for Multi-agent Coordination in Stochastic Environments
paper_authors: Rolando Fernandez, Caleb Probine, Tyler Lee, Jeffrey Chen, Erez Karpas
